what_its_for: This medicine is used to treat multiple myeloma, a type of blood cancer that affects plasma cells in your bone marrow. It may also be used to treat light chain (AL) amyloidosis, a condition where abnormal proteins build up and damage organs. It is usually given along with other cancer medicines as part of a treatment plan designed by your doctor.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as a shot (injection) under your skin, usually in the belly area (abdomen). A healthcare provider will give you this injection in a clinic or hospital setting. You will NOT inject this yourself at home. Each injection takes about 3 to 5 minutes to give. Before each injection, your healthcare team will give you pre-medications (such as antihistamines, steroids, and fever reducers) to help prevent reactions. You will then be watched for at least 30 minutes after each injection to make sure you do not have a bad reaction.
dosing: Your doctor will decide how often you receive this medicine based on your treatment plan and the phase of your therapy. Typically, doses are given more frequently at the start of treatment (for example, weekly or every two weeks) and then less often over time (such as once a month). Do not change your dosing schedule without talking to your doctor first. Always keep your scheduled appointments.
missed_dose: If you miss or have to reschedule an appointment, contact your doctor or healthcare team as soon as possible. They will help you figure out the best time to receive your next dose and adjust your schedule if needed. Do not try to give yourself this medicine at home.
storage: This medicine is stored and handled by your healthcare provider or pharmacy. You do not need to store it at home. If for any reason you are given this medicine to bring to your appointment, keep it refrigerated between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze it. Keep it in the original box to protect it from light, and do not shake it. Keep all medicines out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Tell your healthcare team about ALL medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take before starting treatment, as this drug can interact with other medications. Avoid live vaccines (such as the shingles vaccine Zostavax) during treatment unless your doctor approves. Tell your blood bank or lab that you are taking this medicine before any blood typing or compatibility tests, because it can interfere with certain blood tests (called indirect antiglobulin tests or Coombs tests). Avoid being around people who are sick with infections, as this medicine can weaken your immune system.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: trouble breathing, shortness of breath, or wheezing; severe cough; chest tightness or chest pain; dizziness, lightheadedness, or fainting; severe chills, fever (temperature above 100.4°F or 38°C), or shaking; swelling of your face, lips, throat, or tongue; hives, rash, or severe itching; nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea that will not stop; signs of infection (unusual pain, redness, warmth, or swelling); unusual bruising or bleeding; feeling very tired or weak; or signs of a nerve problem such as numbness or tingling. Also tell your doctor if you become pregnant or plan to become pregnant.
when_it_works: This medicine starts working right away in your body, but it may take several weeks to months before you or your doctor notice the full benefit. Your doctor will monitor your progress with regular blood tests and check-ups. Do not stop treatment early even if you feel well, unless your doctor tells you to.
special_populations: Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: This medicine may harm an unborn baby. Women who can become pregnant should use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 3 months after the last dose. Tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant. It is not known if this medicine passes into breast milk, so breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment and for at least 3 months after the last dose. Older Adults: Older patients (age 65 and above) can use this medicine, but may need closer monitoring for side effects. Kidney or Liver Problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver problems, as this may affect your treatment. Children: The safety and effectiveness of this medicine have not been established in children.
